fathers/tertullian/summary: A highly educated layman of Carthage whose some thirty surviving treatises created much of the Latin theological vocabulary, including 'Trinity', 'person' and 'substance'. Brilliant, rigorist and combative, he defended Christians against Rome, attacked heretics and pagan philosophy ('What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?'), and later joined the New Prophecy, which kept him from being honoured as a saint while his formulas shaped Western doctrine.
fathers/tertullian/story:
Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus was born c. 155–160 in Carthage, the capital of Roman Africa, to a pagan family. Jerome says his father was a centurion and that Tertullian became a presbyter; T. D. Barnes and other historians doubt both claims and also reject the old identification with the jurist Tertullianus cited in the Digest. What is clear is an excellent rhetorical and literary education. He converted c. 195, was married, and wrote between c. 196 and c. 220, the first major Christian author in Latin.

His Apology (197), addressed to the provincial governors, mocks the injustice of trials in which Christians are tortured to deny rather than to confess, and ends with the famous claim that 'the blood of Christians is seed' (Apol. 50). In To Scapula (212) he argued that 'it is a fundamental human right that every person should worship according to his own convictions', an early plea for religious liberty. Treatises On Idolatry, On the Shows and On the Crown forbade Christians to take part in idolatrous trades, the games and, in some circumstances, military service.

Against heretics he used legal argument. The Prescription against Heretics (c. 200) contends that heretics have no right to argue from Scripture at all, since Scripture belongs to the churches founded by the apostles; it also asks 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord between the Academy and the Church?' (ch. 7). Yet Tertullian used Stoic philosophy freely, teaching that the soul is corporeal (On the Soul) and that souls are transmitted from parents (traducianism). His five books Against Marcion defend the unity of the Old and New Testaments; On the Flesh of Christ contains the paradox misremembered as 'credo quia absurdum': 'the Son of God died; it is credible because it is unfitting… he rose; it is certain because impossible' (ch. 5).

Against Praxeas (c. 213), aimed at a Monarchian who said the Father himself suffered, introduced the Latin formula of one substance (substantia) in three persons (personae), and spoke of the Trinitas, 'the unity distributing itself into a trinity'. He described Christ as one person in whom two substances, divine and human, remain unconfused (Prax. 27), language echoed in Leo's Tome and at Chalcedon (451). His Trinitarian thought retained subordinationist elements, but it set the vocabulary for the West.

From c. 207 Tertullian's writings show sympathy with the New Prophecy (Montanism) from Phrygia, with its new revelations of the Paraclete, stricter fasting, rejection of second marriage and refusal to forgive grave sins after baptism (On Modesty). Older accounts said he left the church; recent scholars (Tabbernee, Trevett, Rankin) argue that he belonged to a prophetic group within the Carthaginian church. A sect of 'Tertullianists' survived until Augustine's time. Cyprian called him 'the Master' and read him daily; the later Gelasian Decree listed his works as not to be received. He died after 220, probably c. 225–240.
fathers/tertullian/roots/0/text: His style is a showpiece of Latin rhetoric: paradox, irony, epigram and the techniques of forensic speech learned in Carthage's schools.
fathers/tertullian/roots/1/text: He used legal concepts such as praescriptio (a plea barring an opponent's case), persona, substantia and satisfactio; scholars debate how far these carried technical legal meaning.
fathers/tertullian/roots/2/text: He adopted Stoic materialism (God and the soul as 'body' of a spiritual kind) and called Seneca 'often one of us'.
fathers/tertullian/roots/3/text: Much of his work attacks Valentinians, Marcionites and Docetists, defending the flesh of Christ and the resurrection of the body.
fathers/tertullian/roots/4/text: He drew heavily on Irenaeus (Against the Valentinians), Justin and the Greek apologists.
fathers/tertullian/roots/5/text: He defended the Old Testament against Marcion and read it typologically as foretelling Christ.
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/0: One God in three persons sharing one substance (trinitas, una substantia, tres personae)
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/1: Christ as one person in two substances, divine and human, without confusion
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/2: The rule of faith and apostolic churches as owners of Scripture against heretics
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/3: Rejection of idolatry, the games and compromise with pagan society; religious liberty
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/4: Traducianism and a hereditary 'vice of origin' (vitium originis)
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/5: Rigorism on penance and remarriage; openness to the New Prophecy
fathers/tertullian/keyTeachings/6: Martyrdom as the seed of the church
fathers/tertullian/works/0/note: Defence of Christians addressed to Roman governors; 'the blood of Christians is seed'.
fathers/tertullian/works/1/note: Legal argument that heretics have no claim on Scripture; 'What has Athens to do with Jerusalem?'
fathers/tertullian/works/2/note: Earliest treatise on a sacrament; counsels delay of baptism for small children.
fathers/tertullian/works/3/note: The main ancient refutation of Marcion and principal source for his canon and Antitheses.
fathers/tertullian/works/4/note: Foundational Latin Trinitarian and Christological treatise.
fathers/tertullian/works/5/note: First Christian psychology; corporeal soul and traducianism.
fathers/tertullian/works/6/note: Forbids Christians trades and offices involving idolatry.
fathers/tertullian/doctrineContributions: Coined or first used in theology the Latin terms trinitas, persona and substantia, the basis of Western Trinitarian language.
His 'one person, two substances' formula anticipated Leo's Tome and the Definition of Chalcedon.
His traducianism and idea of an inherited 'vice of origin' prepared the way for Cyprian's and Augustine's doctrine of original sin.
On Baptism is the first treatise on a Christian sacrament and early evidence for (and reservations about) infant baptism.
Argued for freedom of religion and separation from idolatrous public life.
Developed the argument from the rule of faith and the apostolic churches' possession of Scripture.
fathers/tertullian/laterInfluence/0/text: Cyprian treated him as his master; Novatian, Hilary and Augustine inherited his vocabulary, though Augustine rejected his materialism.
fathers/tertullian/laterInfluence/1/text: His terms of satisfaction and merit in penance fed into medieval penitential theology and Anselm's satisfaction language, though the line of influence is indirect.
fathers/tertullian/laterInfluence/2/text: Beatus Rhenanus published the first edition (1521); Reformers cited his Prescription and his appeal to Scripture, while Catholics cited his appeal to apostolic churches.
fathers/tertullian/laterInfluence/3/text: His 'Athens and Jerusalem' became a byword for fideism, and he is studied for early Christian views of women, the military and religious freedom.
fathers/tertullian/reception/0/text: Not canonised because of his Montanism; honoured as an ecclesiastical writer whose terminology became official doctrine.
fathers/tertullian/reception/1/text: Little read in the Greek East; respected as an early writer but not venerated.
fathers/tertullian/reception/2/text: Valued for his defence of Scripture, his Trinitarian vocabulary and his plea for religious liberty; his rigorism and views on women are criticised.
fathers/tertullian/reception/3/text: Some writers see his defence of the New Prophecy as early evidence for continuing prophetic gifts.
fathers/tertullian/controversies/0: Extent and nature of his adherence to the New Prophecy (Montanism)
fathers/tertullian/controversies/1: Whether he was a presbyter, a lawyer or a centurion's son
fathers/tertullian/controversies/2: His views on women ('you are the devil's gateway', On the Apparel of Women 1.1)
fathers/tertullian/controversies/3: Rigorism on penance, remarriage, military service and flight in persecution
fathers/tertullian/controversies/4: Supposed anti-intellectualism ('credo quia absurdum' is a misquotation)
fathers/tertullian/quote/text: What indeed has Athens to do with Jerusalem? What concord is there between the Academy and the Church? What between heretics and Christians?
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/roles/0: Presbyter and rival bishop in Rome
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/summary: Hippolytus (c. 170–c. 235), the last major Christian author at Rome to write in Greek, attacked the Modalists and Pope Callistus, led a rigorist breakaway community, and died a reconciled martyr in the Sardinian mines; a large body of writings — and the much-debated ‘Apostolic Tradition’ — has been attached to his name.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/story:
Little about Hippolytus’ life is certain. Photius reports that he was a disciple of Irenaeus, and his works show Irenaeus’ influence. In the early third century he was a learned presbyter in Rome who opposed the teaching of Noetus and Sabellius that Father and Son were one person in different modes (Modalism or Monarchianism). His Against Noetus defends a distinct Logos who comes forth from the Father for creation and salvation.

The Refutation of All Heresies (Elenchos), recovered at Mount Athos in 1842 and attributed to him by most scholars, accuses Popes Zephyrinus and Callistus (217–222) of favouring Modalism and of laxity in readmitting sinners and recognising marriages between noblewomen and slaves. Its author seems to have led a separate community and is often called the first ‘antipope’. The book traces each heresy to a Greek philosophical school or pagan cult — Valentinus to Pythagoras and Plato, Noetus to Heraclitus — a polemical genealogy that is itself an early ‘borrowing from paganism’ argument.

In 235 the emperor Maximinus Thrax exiled both Pope Pontian and Hippolytus to the mines of Sardinia, where both died; the Liberian Catalogue records that their bodies were brought back to Rome and buried on 13 August, apparently after reconciliation. A seated marble statue found in 1551 on the Via Tiburtina, inscribed with an Easter table and a list of works, was long taken to be his portrait; it was in fact a female philosopher figure reused and restored in the Renaissance.

Scholars since the 1940s (Nautin, Brent, Simonetti) have debated whether ‘Hippolytus’ was one author or two — a Roman presbyter who wrote the Refutation and an Eastern bishop who wrote the exegetical works such as the Commentary on Daniel (the oldest surviving Christian biblical commentary) — or even a ‘school’ of writers. The church order known as the Apostolic Tradition, reconstructed in the early twentieth century and long dated to c. 215, became the template for the Roman Catholic Eucharistic Prayer II (1968) and many Anglican and Protestant liturgical revisions. Paul Bradshaw and colleagues now argue that it is a composite ‘living text’ of various dates and places, not securely Hippolytus’ or Roman.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/roots/0/text: Depends heavily on Irenaeus’ Against Heresies for his catalogue of Gnostic sects and his economy of salvation.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/roots/1/text: The Refutation is an encyclopaedic attack on Gnostic systems, claiming they plagiarise Greek philosophy, astrology and mystery cults.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/roots/2/text: Though hostile to philosophy as the root of heresy, he summarises the Greek schools in detail and uses Stoic-Platonic Logos categories in his own theology.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/roots/3/text: His Commentary on Daniel and works on the Antichrist interpret prophecy and calculate world history, placing the end 500 years after Christ.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/roots/4/text: Presents himself as guardian of the apostolic tradition against innovators, a claim the church-order title later exploited.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/keyTeachings/: The Logos is a distinct person from the Father, against Modalism
Heresies are derived from pagan philosophy and cults rather than scripture
A rigorist discipline for serious post-baptismal sin
Chronological calculation delaying the end of the world (Christ born in the 5500th year; end c. 500 AD)
Typological and prophetic reading of Daniel and the Antichrist
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/works/0/note: Ten books; book 1 long attributed to Origen; rediscovered on Mount Athos in 1842.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/works/1/note: Anti-Modalist treatise defending the distinct Logos.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/works/2/note: The oldest surviving Christian biblical commentary.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/works/3/note: Treatise on eschatology from Daniel and Revelation.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/works/4/note: Church order with ordination prayers, baptismal rite and eucharistic prayer; attribution and date disputed.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/works/5/note: World chronicle to 234, influential on later chronography.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/doctrineContr: Defended the distinction of Father and Son against Modalism, though with an ‘economic’ theology later judged subordinationist.
The Apostolic Tradition, whatever its origin, became a key source for reconstructing early liturgy and inspired 20th-century reforms.
His Antichrist treatise and chronology shaped later apocalyptic calculation.
The Apostolic Tradition describes catechumenate, interrogatory creed and anointings, a major witness to early baptismal practice.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/laterInfluenc: Eucharistic Prayer II of the 1970 Roman Missal and prayers in Anglican, Lutheran and Methodist books are based on the Apostolic Tradition’s anaphora.
His genealogy of heresies from philosophy influenced Epiphanius and later polemic.
Material from the Apostolic Tradition passed into the Apostolic Constitutions, the Canons of Hippolytus and the Ethiopian Testamentum Domini.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/reception/0/t: Venerated as martyr with Pope Pontian (13 August); regarded as reconciled before death despite his schism.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/reception/1/t: Commemorated (30 January and other dates), often conflated with other martyrs of the same name.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/reception/2/t: Chiefly known through the Apostolic Tradition’s influence on modern liturgies.
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/controversies: Schism against Pope Callistus and the charge of being the first antipope
One author or two? The disputed corpus
Authorship, date and Roman provenance of the Apostolic Tradition
Identity of the Via Tiburtina statue
fathers/hippolytus-of-rome/quote/text: It is the Father who commands, and the Son who obeys, and the Holy Spirit who gives understanding.
